Issued at 152 AM CDT Sun Sep 27 2026

A well-defined shortwave/vorticity maximum is evident over 
south-central Iowa on GOES water vapor imagery loops early this
morning, slowly pinwheeling its way eastward towards the 
Mississippi River. Later today, this disturbance will 
eventually run into a wall of dry low-mid-level air and large- 
scale subsidence associated with an expansive ridge that is in 
place over the Great Lakes and portions of Ontario and Quebec, 
and most of its associated precipitation will disintegrate as a
result. Essentially all 00Z and 03Z model guidance suggests 
that this will occur before this precipitation reaches our 
western CWA border, but still couldn't completely rule out a few
sprinkles sneaking into our forecast area as far east as the 
I-39 corridor given that the driving wave looks a bit more 
robust on satellite and radar than this forecast guidance 
suggests it should be at the time of this writing.

Otherwise, temperatures today should be similar to yesterday's 
temperatures, with seasonable highs in the mid 60s to mid 70s
once again. The coolest temperature readings will occur near 
Lake Michigan, courtesy of onshore flow. With little air mass 
change expected into tomorrow as a result of a persisting 
eastern CONUS Rex block, similar temperature readings should be 
observed again on Monday -- though tomorrow's high temperatures 
will likely be a smidge warmer than today's with another day of 
air mass warming and less upper-level cloud cover to contend
with. Additionally, while this air mass remains quite dry, it 
may still nevertheless support patchy fog in portions of our 
area both this morning and again tonight into tomorrow morning 
wherever skies can remain relatively clear amidst light/calm 
winds within a strongly decoupled planetary boundary layer.

The Rex block will likely have broken down by Tuesday, though 
the same air mass will still remain in place across the region,
and another day of incremental air mass warming could allow for
some of our southern locales to make a real push towards 80F 
during the afternoon. The Rex block breaking down will also 
allow for a more progressive weather pattern to take shape 
across the CONUS during the middle and latter portions of the 
week. Of particular relevance for this time period will be a 
deep, positively-tilted longwave trough that is currently 
approaching the Pacific coast. This trough will evolve into a 
cut-off upper low over the Desert Southwest Monday into Tuesday 
while a separate shortwave component of this trough breaks off 
and continues to advance towards the Great Lakes.

This more progressive shortwave disturbance will help induce a 
blossoming axis of rain across an attendant frontal zone from
the central Plains into the Upper Midwest Tuesday into 
Wednesday. There has been a notable slowing and westward trend 
with this frontal zone and the accompanying precipitation axis 
in both the GEFS and GDPS ensemble systems over the past 24
hours. If such a trend were to ultimately be realized, then 
precipitation likely wouldn't arrive in our forecast area until
Wednesday morning at the earliest, and large portions of our 
area (particularly with southeastward extent) could potentially
remain dry altogether on Wednesday. It remains to be seen 
whether the EPS will jump onto this trend as well, but for now, 
the NBM's PoPs have reasonably been slashed into the "chance" 
range across the southeastern half of our forecast area on 
Wednesday where the occurrence of precipitation on this day is 
in more doubt than it was previously.

Regardless of what happens on Wednesday, at least one period of
rain still looks likely to occur here sometime during the 
latter half of the week as the aforementioned upper low and/or 
the remnants of Pacific Hurricane Polo work their way into the 
Midwest in some sort of fashion and induce an influx of 
combined Gulf and Pacific moisture into the region. Ensemble 
guidance still remains all over the place with the timing of 
this rainfall and overall rainfall totals for the region during 
this late week time frame, largely due to a considerable amount 
of uncertainty regarding an expected interaction/phasing attempt
between the upper low and Polo's remnants and the subsequent 
ramifications that will have on the evolution of these 
atmospheric features into the latter half of the week. The 
latest NBM PoPs for our area currently peak in the "likely" 
category on Thursday with broad-brushed chance PoPs then 
continuing into the weekend. This looks reasonable for now, but
will likely need refinement in the coming days as forecast 
trends become clearer.

Ogorek
